newsitem.title: USA: McDonnell Douglas to make commercial C-17 plane.
newsitem.headline: McDonnell Douglas to make commercial C-17 plane.

text.p: McDonnell Douglas Corp. said Tuesday it is planning to produce a commercial version of its C-17 military transport airplane.

McDonnell Douglas spokesman Rick Fuller said production is being ramped up at its Long Beach plant and the company is in discussion with the Federal Aviation Administration to certify the new model which will be called the MD-17 and be used for transporting large cargo.
St. Louis-based McDonnell has been in discussions with customers about the new model. Fuller said there is demand for the new aircraft although no firm orders have yet been placed.
"We have been talking to potential customers and there is interest," Fuller said. "There is a variety of airlines and cargo carriers that might decide to buy this airplane."
Fuller said the increased demand for the plane could come from air cargo carriers, and U.S. and foreign military.

Demand for the new model could be between 35 and 50 aircraft over the next eight to 10 years, Fuller said. He estimated the commercial version of the airplane would cost $200 million, or less, depending on the amount of modification needed.

The C-17 Globemaster 3 was developed for use by the U.S. Air Force. To date 31 of the planes have been delivered under a multi-year contract for 120 planes. McDonnell will produce eight C-17s this year, nine in fiscal 1998, 13 in 1999 before stepping up to 15 a year through 2002. Five planes will be produced in 2003, the last year of the contract.
"We think we will be building them for a lot longer than that because we think it has real potential," Fuller said.
Fuller said McDonnell plans to produce an extra two "white-tail," or unfinished, planes next year in addition to the nine scheduled for the U.S. Air Force.

"This gives us the capability if we do reach a contract on the commercial aircraft, or international sales, that we will have airplanes already being constructed that we can make available," Fuller said.

The outsize cargo ability of the MD-17 will give McDonnell Douglas a full range of cargo airplanes. It also produces the MD-11 and the DC-10 both of which operate in the traditional cargo market. The MD-17 will compete with the older Russian-built Antonov An-124.
The MD-17's biggest advantage is its ability to operate on shorter runways that the An-124. The MD-17 can carry more than 161,000 pounds of cargo and land on less than 3,000 feet.
Fuller said that capability makes the plane ideal for transporting oil rigs, construction equipment and other infrastructure loads that may need to be delivered to remote locations.

The C-17 would need a number of modifications to transform it into the MD-17. The air-drop system, used to drop paratroopers from the plane, the seats and the air refueling system would need to be removed among other things.

By increasing production now McDonnell hopes to avoid a potential lengthy backlog once new orders are placed because each aircraft takes between 16 and 18 months to make. Fuller also said the heightened activity would "stabilize" the work force at the Long Beach plant, which may have seen some fluctuation without the higher output.
McDonnell agreed to merge with Seattle-based Boeing Co. in December in a stock deal valued at about $15 billion.
